title: Forms of Ownership
summary: Sole traders, partnerships, companies and other forms of business ownership, limited and unlimited liability, and the advantages and disadvantages of each.

notes.text: Why the form of ownership matters

When starting a business, an entrepreneur must choose a **form of ownership**. This decides who owns and controls the business, how much capital can be raised, who shares the profit, and who is responsible for the business's debts.
The owners are personally responsible for all the debts of the business. If the business cannot pay, the owners' personal possessions (house, car) can be sold to pay the creditors.
The owners can lose only the money they invested in the business; their personal possessions are protected.
A business with legal personality exists separately from its owners in law: it can own property, sign contracts, sue and be sued in its own name, and continues even if owners change (continuity).

notes.label: Exam tip
notes.text: Look at the name of a business: **(Pty) Ltd** = private company; **Ltd** = public company; **NPC** = non-profit company; **Inc.** = personal liability company (used by professionals such as attorneys).

questions.prompt: Give TWO advantages and TWO disadvantages of a sole trader.
questions.memo:
Advantages (1 each): easy and cheap to start; quick decisions; keeps all profit; personal contact
Disadvantages (1 each): unlimited liability; limited capital; all risk and workload; no continuity

questions.prompt: Why can a partnership be risky for its partners?
questions.memo:
✓ Partners have unlimited liability (1)
✓ and are responsible for debts caused by the decisions of the other partners / disagreements can arise (1)

questions.prompt: Why can a public company raise more capital than a sole trader?
questions.memo:
✓ It can sell shares to the public (1)
✓ to many investors, who are attracted by limited liability (1)
